title_en: Zhongjing Industrial (Group) Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Electric Power Industrial Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over equity transfer
ruling_gist_en: Although the transfer of state-owned property rights must be conducted through public trading at a property rights exchange, since the property rights exchange does not have the authority to determine legal matters such as whether a party has lost its preemptive right, and in the absence of explicit legal provisions and without the shareholder expressly waiving the preemptive right, a shareholder who enjoys the preemptive right but fails to enter the exchange for trading cannot be deemed to have lost that right based on the exchange's self-established trading rule that 'failure to enter the exchange is deemed waiver of the preemptive right.'

full_text_en:
Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Electric Power Industry Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over equity transfer

Ruling Summary

Although the transfer of state-owned property rights shall be conducted publicly through a property rights exchange, the property rights exchange does not have the authority to determine legal matters such as whether a party has lost its preemptive right. In the absence of explicit legal provisions and where the shareholder has not expressly waived its preemptive right, the fact that a shareholder entitled to such right fails to enter the exchange for trading does not lead to the conclusion that its preemptive right has been lost, based solely on the exchange’s self-established rule that “failure to enter the exchange is deemed a waiver of the preemptive right.”

Plaintiff: Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. XXX, Luocheng Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Gao Yang, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Defendant: Shanghai Electric Power Industry Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. XXX, Ningbo Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Xu Jingguo, General Manager of the company.

Defendant: China Water Resources and Electric Power Materials Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. XXX, Fuxingmenwai Street, Xicheng District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Zheng Wenyuan, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Third Party: Shanghai New Energy Environmental Protection Engineering Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. XXX, Jiangxi Middle Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Zhu Kaiqing, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Third Party: Shanghai United Assets and Equity Exchange, domiciled at No. XXX, Guangdong Road, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Cai Minyong, President of the exchange.

The plaintiff, Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongjing Company), filed an action with the Huangpu District People’s Court of Shanghai against the defendants, Shanghai Electric Power Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Electric Power Company), China Water Resources and Electric Power Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Water Resources Company), and the third parties, Shanghai New Energy Environmental Protection Engineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as New Energy Company) and Shanghai United Assets and Equity Exchange (hereinafter referred to as the Exchange), concerning a dispute over equity transfer.

The plaintiff, Zhongjing Company, alleged: The plaintiff and the defendant Electric Power Company were shareholders of the third party New Energy Company, holding 38.2% and 61.8% of the shares respectively. On June 1, 2012, without the consent of Zhongjing Company, Electric Power Company listed its shares for trading on the Exchange. On July 2, Zhongjing Company raised an objection to the third party Exchange, explicitly stating its retention of the preemptive right and requesting to suspend the transaction for a new information disclosure. However, in order to prevent Zhongjing Company from exercising its preemptive right, Electric Power Company entered into a property rights transfer contract with Water Resources Company on July 3, before Water Resources Company had paid the deposit, and the entire transaction was completed during the period when the Exchange was reviewing Zhongjing Company’s objection. The Exchange did not serve Zhongjing Company with a notice of decision not to suspend the transaction until July 6. Zhongjing Company argued that Electric Power Company’s unauthorized transfer of shares infringed upon its shareholder preemptive right, and that the determination by Water Resources Company and the Exchange that Zhongjing Company had waived its preemptive right due to its failure to enter the exchange had no legal basis. Therefore, Zhongjing Company requested a judgment: that Zhongjing Company had a preemptive right over the 61.8% equity interest in New Energy Company transferred between Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company, and that it should exercise that preemptive right at the transfer price of RMB 48,691,000 (all currency below is in RMB). During the trial, Zhongjing Company expressed its willingness to accept the terms of the transfer contract between Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company.

The defendant, Electric Power Company, argued: The external transfer of equity was approved by a shareholders’ resolution of the third party New Energy Company on February 15, 2012, and the plaintiff Zhongjing Company also expressed consent. As a collectively-owned enterprise, Electric Power Company was required by relevant laws to transfer its equity through listing on a property rights exchange. After receiving the listing notice, Zhongjing Company did not exercise its rights at the Exchange, which amounted to a waiver of its preemptive right. Therefore, its claims were unfounded.

The defendant, Water Resources Company, argued: The plaintiff Zhongjing Company was negligent in exercising its rights at the third party Exchange and had already waived its preemptive right. The equity transaction between Water Resources Company and the defendant Electric Power Company was lawful, fair, and just. Water Resources Company had already paid the equity transfer price and fulfilled the ancillary conditions for the transfer. The legitimate rights of Water Resources Company as a bona fide third party should be protected by law. Therefore, it disagreed with Zhongjing Company’s claims.

The third party New Energy Company submitted its opinion: The transaction process at the third party Exchange was lawful, and the defendant Water Resources Company had obtained shareholder status in New Energy Company.

The third party Exchange submitted its opinion: The Exchange fully complied with the trading rules, and the project information disclosure was truthful, accurate, and complete. The plaintiff Zhongjing Company only requested a suspension of the transaction on the last day of the listing period on the grounds that the materials submitted by the defendant Electric Power Company contained significant omissions and that there was a dispute over ownership. Upon verification, these claims were false. The acquisition of equity by the defendant Water Resources Company was lawful and valid. The State-Owned Assets Law stipulates that the transfer of state-owned assets shall be conducted publicly at a property rights exchange. The prerequisite for Zhongjing Company to exercise its preemptive right is “under the same conditions,” which includes both procedural and substantive equivalence. The procedure for the transfer of state-owned property rights requires that the parties enter the exchange for trading. By refusing to enter the exchange, Zhongjing Company was deemed to have waived its preemptive right; otherwise, it would violate the procedural equivalence requirement under the “same conditions” principle.

The Huangpu District People’s Court of Shanghai found the following facts in the first instance:

The third party New Energy Company was established on March 16, 1999. The original shareholders were Shanghai Electric Power General Company (later renamed Electric Power Company), Shanghai Industrial Investment (Group) Co., Ltd., Shanghai Environmental Protection Engineering Complete Set Co., Ltd., and China Zhongjing Energy Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongjing Energy), holding 45%, 10%, 6.8%, and 38.2% of the shares respectively.

On February 10, 2010, the defendant Electric Power Company and Zhongjing Energy signed the “Framework Agreement on Capital Increase and Equity Adjustment of New Energy Company” (hereinafter referred to as the Framework Agreement), stipulating: The two parties would jointly acquire the shares of Shanghai Industrial Investment (Group) Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Environmental Protection Engineering Complete Set Co., Ltd., such that the equity ratios of Electric Power Company and Zhongjing Energy would become 51% and 49% respectively; Zhongjing Energy would transfer its 38.2% equity interest to Zhongjing Company as soon as possible, converting New Energy Company into a domestic-invested company.

In May 2010, the plaintiff Zhongjing Company replaced Zhongjing Energy as a shareholder of the third party New Energy Company. On August 6, the defendant Electric Power Company and Zhongjing Company signed a supplementary agreement, stipulating: Electric Power Company would first fund the acquisition of the 16.8% equity interests held by Shanghai Industrial Investment (Group) Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Environmental Protection Engineering Complete Set Co., Ltd. in New Energy Company, resulting in Electric Power Company’s and Zhongjing Company’s equity ratios in New Energy Company becoming 61.8% and 38.2% respectively; after the acquisition, Electric Power Company would transfer 10.8% of the equity in New Energy Company to Zhongjing Company under the same conditions, or during the capital increase process, the parties would adjust the equity ratio to 51% for Electric Power Company and 49% for Zhongjing Company based on the specific circumstances, ultimately adjusting the equity ratio to 50% each in accordance with the Framework Agreement. On December 1, the third party Exchange issued a property rights transaction certificate for Electric Power Company’s acquisition of the 16.8% equity interest in New Energy Company from Shanghai Industrial Investment (Group) Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Environmental Protection Engineering Complete Set Co., Ltd.

On February 15, 2012, the third party New Energy Company passed a shareholders’ resolution with the following contents: 1. Approved Electric Power Company’s transfer of its 61.8% equity interest, with the transfer price based on the appraisal value; 2. Zhongjing Company would not waive its preemptive right; 3. The relevant procedures for the equity transfer would be handled by the parties in accordance with legal procedures; 4. After the equity transfer, the company’s articles of association and shareholders’ capital contribution records would be amended accordingly; 5. Entrusted Shanghai Hujinmao Certified Public Accountants Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Dongzhou Asset Valuation Co., Ltd. to conduct a financial audit and asset appraisal; 6. The appraisal base date was December 31, 2011.

On May 25, 2012, the third party New Energy Company submitted the materials for the public transfer of equity to the third party Exchange. On June 1, the Exchange published information on the transfer of 61.8% equity in New Energy Company: the listing period was from June 1 to July 2, 2012; under “Equity Structure of the Target Enterprise,” it was indicated that the existing shareholder had not waived the right of first refusal; “Transaction Conditions” included a listing price of RMB 48,691,000, a one-time payment, continuation of the target company employees’ labor contracts, support for the long-term development of the target company, and promotion of the target company’s performance growth; prospective transferees should pay a deposit of RMB 14 million to the Exchange within three working days after qualification confirmation, failing which they would be deemed to have waived the right to receive the transfer; if only one qualified prospective transferee was solicited at the end of the listing period, the transaction would be concluded through agreement, with the deposit serving as part of the equity transfer price; if two or more qualified prospective transferees were solicited, the transferee would be determined through a bidding process; the prospective transferee was required, within one working day after the Exchange issued the property rights transaction certificate, to repay the target company’s debt of RMB 35 million owed to the transferor on behalf of the target company. If other shareholders of the target company intended to participate in the transfer, they should submit a transfer application to the Exchange during the period of the property rights transfer information announcement and exercise the preemptive right as a priority under the same conditions at the bidding site; otherwise, they would be deemed to have waived the transfer.

The defendant Electric Power Company notified the plaintiff Zhongjing Company of the relevant listing information via SMS, express mail, notarization, and other means.

On July 2, the plaintiff Zhongjing Company sent a letter to the Exchange, stating that, based on the Framework Agreement and the supplementary agreement, the information disclosure regarding the disputed equity transfer was incomplete, there was a dispute over ownership, and Zhongjing Company had a preemptive right. It requested the third party Exchange to suspend the listing and re-disclose the information.

On July 3, the defendant Water Resources Company and the defendant Electric Power Company signed a property rights transfer contract with the following contents: The subject matter of the contract was the 61.8% equity interest in New Energy Company held by Electric Power Company; the value of the subject property rights and the transaction price between the parties was RMB 48,691,000; the price (including the deposit) was to be paid in a lump sum within five working days after signing the contract; the new target company was to continue performing the labor contracts of the original target company’s employees; within one working day after the third party Exchange issued the transaction certificate, Water Resources Company was required to repay the third party New Energy Company’s debt of RMB 35 million owed to Electric Power Company, paying it in a lump sum to the account designated by Electric Power Company, etc. The following day, the Exchange issued a property rights transaction certificate, and Water Resources Company fulfilled its obligations for the equity transfer price and debt assumption. On the same day, the Exchange issued a decision not to suspend the transaction to the plaintiff Zhongjing Company, stating: Upon review, the equity transfer procedures complied with the relevant provisions on property rights transactions, and therefore the Exchange decided not to approve Zhongjing Company’s application. On September 11, New Energy Company issued a capital contribution certificate to Water Resources Company and included it in the company’s register of shareholders, but the change in industrial and commercial registration was not completed.

The Huangpu District People’s Court of Shanghai held in the first instance:

First, the shareholder’s preemptive right is a statutory right granted by the Company Law. Article 73 of the Company Law of the PRC only provides that in the compulsory execution procedure of a court, if the shareholder with the preemptive right does not exercise it within the statutory period after being notified, it is deemed to have waived the preemptive right. The Company Law and judicial interpretations do not provide for a forfeiture procedure under other circumstances. Second, according to the Supreme People’s Court’s Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC (for Trial Implementation), the effect of silence as a form of implicit expression can only be deemed as a manifestation of intent when provided by law or agreed upon by the parties. Third, as a property rights transaction platform established by law, the Exchange is not vested with the authority to determine legal matters such as whether the subject matter of the transaction is subject to ownership disputes or whether a party has lost its preemptive right.

In summary, in the absence of explicit legal provisions and where the plaintiff Zhongjing Company had not expressly waived its preemptive right, the mere fact that Zhongjing Company did not enter the exchange for trading does not lead to the conclusion that its preemptive right had been lost. From the perspective of commercial transactions, while commercial transactions must follow efficiency principles, they must also take into account the protection of the interests of the transaction participants. Moreover, if the shareholder with the preemptive right does not enter the exchange, the third party Exchange could notify it to express its intention on whether to accept the finally determined price within a certain period; non-attendance does not necessarily hinder the efficiency of the transaction. If undue emphasis is placed on the concept that the non-attendance of the preemptive right shareholder results in the loss of the preemptive right, this would inevitably highlight the protection of the Exchange’s interests and the interests of bona fide third parties, while weakening the protection of the preemptive right shareholder’s interests, leading to an imbalance of interests.

The plaintiff Zhongjing Company raised an objection before the equity transaction, and the third party Exchange should have responded promptly. With reference to the relevant provisions of the “Operating Rules for the Transfer of State-Owned Enterprise Property Rights,” during the information announcement period, if circumstances affecting the normal conduct of the transaction arise, or if an interested party submits a written application and relevant materials for suspension of the information announcement, the property rights transaction institution may decide to suspend the information announcement. For a preemptive right shareholder who has raised an objection, if it has not been promptly informed by the Exchange of the response to its objection, it is unaware whether the transaction will proceed as scheduled, and therefore its non-attendance cannot be deemed as a waiver of its right to receive the transfer. Therefore, in the absence of an explicit waiver of the preemptive right by Zhongjing Company, the equity transfer contract between the defendant Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company is not effective.

Since there are no specific legal provisions on the exercise of the preemptive right beyond the “same conditions” requirement under the Company Law, and there is no precedent for reference in judicial practice, considering the current actual situation of the third party New Energy Company, and in order to prevent abuse of the shareholder preemptive right (i.e., exercising the right but failing to act, rendering the protection of the preemptive right meaningless or causing harm to the interests of the transferor and transferee), it is necessary to determine the period and method for exercising the shareholder’s preemptive right. By analogy with Article 73 of the Company Law, the court held that the plaintiff Zhongjing Company could be required to exercise its right within twenty days after the confirmation takes effect; otherwise, it would be deemed to have waived the right. Only if Zhongjing Company waives its right would the equity transfer contract between the defendant Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company become effective. Regarding the method of exercise, Zhongjing Company should comply with the provisions on the transfer of state-owned assets. In conclusion, Zhongjing Company’s claim that it had a preemptive right over the 61.8% equity interest in New Energy Company transferred between Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company, and its request to exercise that right, were legally grounded and should be supported. The content and conditions for its exercise should be the same as those in the property rights transfer contract between Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company.

Accordingly, the Huangpu District People’s Court of Shanghai, pursuant to Article 72, paragraph 3 and Article 73 of the Company Law of the PRC, Article 54, paragraph 2 of the Enterprise State-Owned Assets Law of the PRC, and Article 66 of the Supreme People’s Court’s Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC (for Trial Implementation), rendered the following judgment on September 25, 2014:

The plaintiff Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. has a preemptive right over the equity interest in the third party Shanghai New Energy Environmental Protection Engineering Co., Ltd. transferred between the defendant Shanghai Electric Power Industry Co., Ltd. and the defendant China Water Resources and Electric Power Materials Co., Ltd.; the plaintiff Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. shall exercise its preemptive right within twenty days from the date this judgment takes effect; otherwise, it will be deemed to have waived the right; the content and conditions for the exercise of the preemptive right by the plaintiff Zhongjing Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. shall be the same as those in the property rights transfer contract signed between the defendant Shanghai Electric Power Industry Co., Ltd. and the defendant China Water Resources and Electric Power Materials Co., Ltd.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, both Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company were dissatisfied and appealed to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People’s Court.

The appellant Electric Power Company appealed, arguing: The appellee Zhongjing Company failed to actively exercise its shareholder preemptive right by entering the exchange within the prescribed period, and thus had lost that right; Zhongjing Company’s reason for requesting a suspension of the transaction on the last day of the Exchange’s listing announcement period violated the principle of good faith and should not be protected by law. On these grounds, Electric Power Company claimed that the first-instance judgment was erroneous, and requested its reversal and a new judgment dismissing all of Zhongjing Company’s claims in the original trial.

The appellant Water Resources Company appealed, arguing: In the absence of any legal provision, the first-instance court created a forfeiture procedure on its own, which was logically flawed and involved errors in the application of law; there was no fact that Electric Power Company or Water Resources Company had infringed upon the appellee Zhongjing Company’s shareholder preemptive right; rather, Zhongjing Company had maliciously obstructed the normal equity transaction. The first-instance judgment unilaterally emphasized the protection of the shareholder preemptive right, but harmed the normal transaction order and the principle of fairness. On these grounds, Water Resources Company also claimed that the first-instance judgment was erroneous, and requested its reversal and a new judgment dismissing all of Zhongjing Company’s claims in the original trial.

The appellants Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company each recognized and concurred with the other’s appeal grounds and factual basis.

The appellee Zhongjing Company argued: The essence of this case was that the appellant Electric Power Company had infringed upon Zhongjing Company’s shareholder preemptive right. Electric Power Company had never notified Zhongjing Company of the specific circumstances of the proposed transfer, including the identity of the proposed transferee; Zhongjing Company had already raised an objection with the Exchange during the listing announcement period, requesting the Exchange to suspend the listing; therefore, Zhongjing Company had not lost its shareholder preemptive right. On the contrary, after receiving Zhongjing Company’s application, the Exchange failed to respond promptly and instead facilitated the completion of the transaction between Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company, which clearly infringed upon Zhongjing Company’s shareholder preemptive right. Zhongjing Company endorsed the first-instance judgment.

The first-instance third party New Energy Company and the first-instance third party Exchange both recognized the appeal requests of the appellants Electric Power Company and Water Resources Company.

The Shanghai Second Intermediate People’s Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai Second Intermediate People’s Court held in the second instance:

The issue in dispute in this case was whether the appellee Zhongjing Company had lost its shareholder preemptive right over the equity interest in question.

The court held that Zhongjing Company had not lost its shareholder preemptive right over the equity interest in question.

First, considering the person-close nature of limited liability companies, the Company Law of the PRC and other relevant laws and regulations provide that when a shareholder transfers equity to a person other than the other shareholders, it shall fully perform the obligation of notification to the other shareholders. The other shareholders have a preemptive right under the same conditions. The content of the notification required here should include the number of shares to be transferred, the price, the method of performance, the circumstances of the proposed transferee, and other key transfer conditions. In this case, first, after the appellant Electric Power Company expressed its intention to transfer equity at the shareholders’ meeting of the first-instance third party New Energy Company, the appellee Zhongjing Company explicitly stated that it did not waive its preemptive right. Second, after Electric Power Company decided to transfer the equity to the appellant Water Resources Company, it also failed to inform Zhongjing Company of the specific circumstances of the proposed transferee. This created an obstacle to Zhongjing Company’s timely and lawful exercise of its right. Since the waiver of a right requires an express indication, it cannot be automatically concluded that Zhongjing Company had waived or lost its shareholder preemptive right.

Second, the appellee Zhongjing Company raised an objection during the listing period of the first-instance third party, the Property Rights Exchange, and explicitly raised the issue of the shareholders' preemptive right, requesting the Property Rights Exchange to suspend the listing transaction. However, the Property Rights Exchange failed to provide timely feedback and instead facilitated the transaction between the appellant Electric Power Company and Water Conservancy Company. Only after the transaction was completed did it notify Zhongjing Company that the transaction would not be suspended. This practice was clearly inappropriate. It should be noted that the Property Rights Exchange is a public institution established with the approval of the municipal government, operating on a non-profit basis, solely providing venue facilities and market services for property rights transactions, and collecting service fees in accordance with regulations. As such, the Property Rights Exchange is not a judicial body and does not have the authority to handle legal disputes; it is not empowered to make legal determinations on whether Zhongjing Company enjoys a preemptive right. Therefore, when Zhongjing Company, as a shareholder of New Energy Company, raised an objection with the Property Rights Exchange during the listing period, the Property Rights Exchange should have suspended the listing transaction. It would have been more reasonable and appropriate to resume the transaction only after the dispute among the shareholders of New Energy Company was resolved in accordance with the law. Consequently, it should not have unilaterally determined whether the objections raised by the other shareholders of the target company were valid, nor should its trading rules conflict with or contradict legal provisions.

In summary, the facts found in the first instance were clear, and the judgment was not improper. Accordingly, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on April 22, 2015:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
